Ayatollah Khomeini. The supreme leader and principal architect of the Iranian Islamic Revolution, who transformed Iran from a secular autocracy into an Islamic theocracy. Khomeini was exiled in Iraq and France for fifteen years, from nineteen sixty-four to nineteen seventy-nine, for opposing the Shah's Western-oriented reforms. He became the symbol of Shiite resistance during that time. When the Shah fell in February nineteen seventy-nine, Khomeini returned to Iran and the Islamic Revolution installed him as supreme leader, the highest authority in the nation. He established the concept of wilayat al-faqih, which means rule by the jurist—a new form of governance that placed a senior Islamic jurist, himself, above elected officials and the constitution. Declaring war on what he called the Great Satan, the United States, and the Little Satan, Israel, he sponsored anti-Israeli and anti-American movements across the region. In nineteen eighty, he initiated the Iran-Iraq War in response to Iraqi invasions, a conflict that became a bloody stalemate killing hundreds of thousands over the next eight years. In nineteen eighty-nine, he issued a fatwa against author Salman Rushdie over alleged blasphemy, establishing a precedent for religious condemnation of intellectuals. When he died in June nineteen eighty-nine, his legacy had reshaped Iran's political system and inspired Shiite movements across Iraq, Lebanon, and beyond.
